a.explanation: Nystatin is a polyene macrolide too toxic for systemic use — it is used topically/orally (not absorbed) for local candidal infections (oral thrush, vaginal candidiasis, skin). Amphotericin B is the systemic polyene; clotrimazole and terbinafine are not polyenes.

Ketoconazole is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor. Astemizole is metabolized by CYP3A4; inhibition raises its plasma level → QT prolongation and torsades de pointes. Terbinafine, fluconazole (weaker) and griseofulvin are much less implicated.

Fluconazole is small, water-soluble and weakly protein-bound — it penetrates CSF well (70%+ of plasma level), unlike ketoconazole and itraconazole (poor CNS penetration). Griseofulvin concentrates in keratin, not CSF.
Saquinavir, indinavir and ritonavir are all protease inhibitors that are both substrates and inhibitors of CYP3A4 — all three promote CYP450 drug-drug interactions (ritonavir most potently).

Ritonavir is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor; fluoxetine is partly metabolized by CYP3A4 (mainly CYP2D6), so ritonavir can raise its serum concentration. Didanosine, amantadine and lamivudine do not inhibit CYP enzymes.
Famciclovir is a prodrug that undergoes first-pass metabolism (deacetylation + oxidation) to the active antiviral penciclovir. Acyclovir, ganciclovir and cidofovir are active as given.

Cidofovir is nephrotoxic; probenecid (with saline hydration) reduces its renal tubular uptake and prevents nephrotoxicity — probenecid is given with each dose. Foscarnet is also nephrotoxic but is not protected by probenecid.

Ganciclovir is monophosphorylated by the CMV-encoded UL97 protein kinase (phosphotransferase) in CMV-infected cells and by viral thymidine kinase in HSV-infected cells; host kinases then add two more phosphates to the active triphosphate.
Vidarabine (ara-A) is deaminated to the hypoxanthine metabolite (ara-Hx) and excreted renally; it is used topically for herpetic keratoconjunctivitis (ointment) and i.v. for HSV encephalitis.
Praziquantel is the drug of choice for all Schistosoma species (including S. haematobium) — it increases Ca2+ permeability of the schistosome tegument → spastic paralysis and death.

Niclosamide is the classic drug for tapeworm (cestode) infections including Taenia saginata — it inhibits mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation in the scolex. Mebendazole is mainly for nematodes, ivermectin for filariae/strongyloidiasis.

Fluconazole (an azole) inhibits fungal 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51), blocking conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol — the essential fungal membrane sterol. The other mechanisms belong to beta-lactams and antivirals.
Trifluridine is a topical pyrimidine nucleoside used for herpes simplex keratitis (1% ophthalmic drops). Zanamivir is anti-influenza, amantadine anti-influenza, indinavir an HIV protease inhibitor.

Metronidazole is the treatment of choice for trichomoniasis (and giardiasis, amoebiasis). Emetine is for invasive amoebiasis, pentamidine for Pneumocystis/leishmaniasis, pyrimethamine for toxoplasmosis/malaria.

Pyrantel pamoate is the drug of choice for ascariasis (and enterobiasis) — it depolarizes nematode muscle (nicotinic agonist) causing spastic paralysis. Praziquantel and niclosamide are for flukes/tapeworms; ivermectin mainly for filariae.

Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) is the drug of choice for filariasis including Wuchereria bancrofti — it immobilizes and sensitizes microfilariae to phagocytosis. Praziquantel, pyrantel and bithionol are for other helminths.
Ribavirin (aerosolized) is the treatment for severe RSV bronchiolitis in infants. Amantadine is anti-influenza A, famciclovir anti-herpes, indinavir an HIV PI.

Chloroquine concentrates in the parasite digestive vacuole and inhibits heme polymerase, preventing detoxification of heme — raising vacuole pH and causing toxic heme accumulation. The other mechanisms describe other antimalarials.

Primaquine causes oxidative hemolysis in G6PD-deficient patients (and methemoglobinemia) — hence the mandatory G6PD test before use. Atovaquone, mefloquine and proguanil do not carry this hemolytic risk.

Primaquine is the only agent that kills the hepatic hypnozoites of P. vivax/P. ovale — eradicating the dormant liver stage and preventing relapse. Artemether-lumefantrine, quinolones and doxycycline are blood/tissue schizonticides without hypnozoitocidal activity.

Quinine causes cinchonism — tinnitus, vertigo, dizziness, nausea — and QT interval prolongation (risk of arrhythmia). Chloroquine can also prolong QT but the classic 'vertigo + QTc' picture in this regimen points to quinine.

Cobicistat is a pure pharmacokinetic booster: it has NO antiviral activity but potently inhibits CYP3A4, prolonging the action of co-administered protease inhibitors (reducing pill burden). Low-dose ritonavir is the alternative booster but does have antiviral activity.

A standard cART regimen is 2 NRTIs + a third agent. With zidovudine as one NRTI and lopinavir/ritonavir as the PI, the best additional component is a second NRTI (emtricitabine). Atazanavir would be a redundant second PI; raltegravir is possible but the classical complete answer is a second NRTI.

Zidovudine and stavudine are both thymidine-analogue NRTIs — they antagonize each other's phosphorylation and combine to increase mitochondrial toxicity; this combination is avoided. Lamivudine (NRTI), nelfinavir (PI) and nevirapine (NNRTI) are compatible with zidovudine.

NNRTIs (especially nevirapine) classically cause skin rashes — including severe Stevens-Johnson syndrome. Insulin resistance, lipodystrophy and mitochondrial toxicity are associated with PIs and NRTIs.

Protease inhibitors cause the metabolic syndrome: lipodystrophy (fat redistribution), hyperlipidemia, insulin resistance/hyperglycemia. Myelosuppression (zidovudine), pancreatitis and peripheral neuropathy are more typical of NRTIs.

NRTIs inhibit mitochondrial DNA polymerase gamma → mitochondrial dysfunction → neuropathy, pancreatitis, cardiomyopathy, hepatic steatosis and lactic acidosis. This is the class-specific mechanism of these toxicities.

Nevirapine is an NNRTI: it binds non-competitively to a hydrophobic pocket near the RT active site and does NOT require intracellular phosphorylation to the triphosphate. NRTIs (lamivudine, stavudine) require phosphorylation; indinavir is a protease inhibitor.

Maraviroc is the CCR5 co-receptor antagonist — it binds the host CCR5 protein, blocking entry of CCR5-tropic HIV; it is ineffective against CXCR4-tropic strains (hence the tropism test). Enfuvirtide is a fusion inhibitor, efavirenz an NNRTI, tenofovir an NRTI.

Baloxavir marboxil is the cap-dependent endonuclease (PA subunit) inhibitor used for influenza — it blocks viral mRNA synthesis. Oseltamivir/zanamivir are neuraminidase inhibitors; rimantadine is an M2 blocker.

Zanamivir is the inhaled (intranasal/oral inhalation) neuraminidase inhibitor, suitable for children who cannot swallow tablets. Oseltamivir is oral, amantadine oral, salbutamol is a bronchodilator not an antiviral.

Valganciclovir is the oral prodrug of ganciclovir (taken twice daily) for CMV retinitis; its dose-limiting toxicity is bone marrow suppression (leucopenia, anemia, thrombocytopenia) requiring blood monitoring. Foscarnet is i.v.; trifluridine is topical for HSV keratitis.

Foscarnet's major dose-limiting toxicity is nephrotoxicity (reversible acute renal failure); it also causes electrolyte disturbances (hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia) and genital ulceration. It is not myelosuppressive.

The adamantanes (amantadine, rimantadine) are no longer recommended by the CDC for influenza due to widespread resistance (M2 channel mutations). Oseltamivir remains recommended; adefovir and entecavir are hepatitis drugs.

Liposomal amphotericin B binds ergosterol in the fungal membrane, forming pores → leakage of cellular components and cell death — used for resistant candidiasis. Clotrimazole and nystatin are topical; terbinafine inhibits squalene epoxidase.
The acute infusion-related reaction — chills, fever, vomiting, hypotension — is characteristic of amphotericin B. Caspofungin, fluconazole and flucytosine do not typically cause this reaction.

a.answer: Fluconazole is a CYP P-450 inhibitor, and can decrease the metabolism of other drugs
a.explanation: Fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9/2C19/3A4. Reviewing her medication list is needed because fluconazole can decrease metabolism of her oral contraceptive (and any other CYP substrates) — raising levels and risking adverse effects.

Flucytosine is converted to 5-fluorouracil, which inhibits thymidylate synthase and is incorporated into RNA/DNA — disrupting DNA synthesis. Amphotericin B already targets the membrane (ergosterol); the second target in the combination is nucleic acid synthesis.

Terbinafine (oral) is the best choice for onychomycosis/dermatophytosis — an allylamine that inhibits fungal squalene epoxidase, depleting ergosterol. Amphotericin B and caspofungin are i.v.; ketoconazole is less effective and more toxic for nails.

After 2 weeks of induction (amphotericin B + flucytosine), oral fluconazole is the standard consolidation/maintenance agent for cryptococcal meningitis (continued for up to a year). It is well absorbed orally with excellent CSF penetration.
Voriconazole is the drug of choice for invasive aspergillosis (better efficacy and survival than amphotericin B). Fluconazole lacks anti-Aspergillus activity; griseofulvin is for dermatophytes.

Fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9, decreasing warfarin metabolism → elevated INR and bleeding (bloody stools, weakness). The patient's warfarin-vitamin K balance is also relevant, but the recent fluconazole initiation explains the acute change — a drug-drug interaction.

Leucovorin (folinic acid) bypasses the dihydrofolate reductase blockade, preventing the megaloblastic anemia/pancytopenia caused by pyrimethamine (a folate antagonist) — without reducing its antiparasitic efficacy.

a.answer: Have blood schizonticidal activity against P falciparum (some species)
a.explanation: Sulfonamides/sulfones (e.g., sulfadoxine, dapsone) are slow blood schizonticides against P. falciparum (combined with pyrimethamine as SP); they have negligible activity against P. vivax blood schizonts and act slowly (not rapid onset).

Ivermectin is used for prophylaxis and treatment of onchocerciasis ('river blindness') — it kills microfilariae and prevents ocular migration. Diethylcarbamazine is contraindicated in onchocerciasis (severe Mazzotti reaction); albendazole and oxamniquine are not used here.

a.answer: The reaction is due to killing of microfilariae
a.explanation: The severe reaction (fever, rash, myalgia, hypotension, edema) after treating onchocerciasis is the Mazzotti reaction — an inflammatory response to the massive killing of microfilariae (not drug toxicity). It is managed with antihistamines/corticosteroids and symptomatic care.

a.answer: Kills adult worms in the colon but not the eggs
a.explanation: Pyrantel pamoate is a depolarizing neuromuscular blocker that paralyzes adult nematodes (roundworm, pinworm) in the colon; it does not kill eggs. It acts on nicotinic receptors (not GABA — that is ivermectin), and is not used for tapeworms or flukes.

a.answer: If the patient has a history of seizure disorders, hospitalizationis recommended during treatment
a.explanation: Oxamniquine can cause CNS effects including convulsions — hospitalization is recommended during treatment in patients with a history of seizures. The other statements are inaccurate (it is effective in chronic disease, unsafe in pregnancy, and only for S. mansoni).

Hydatid disease (Echinococcus granulosus) does not respond to praziquantel — it is treated with albendazole (plus surgery/PAIR). Praziquantel is effective for opisthorchiasis (flukes), pork tapeworm and schistosomiasis.

Ivermectin enhances GABA-mediated (and glutamate-gated chloride) transmission, causing flaccid paralysis of nematodes. Pyrantel pamoate is a nicotinic depolarizer; albendazole inhibits microtubule assembly; DEC affects microfilariae.

Niclosamide is effective against cestodes (tapeworms) including Taenia solium and Taenia saginata. Ascaris (nematode) → pyrantel/albendazole; Echinococcus (hydatid) → albendazole; Fasciola hepatica → triclabendazole.

Albendazole is a broad-spectrum benzimidazole effective against both Ascaris lumbricoides and hookworms (Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale) — ideal for this mixed infection. Ivermectin, niclosamide and praziquantel are not the best choices for these nematodes.

Oseltamivir (neuraminidase inhibitor) provides additional antiviral protection against circulating influenza, including in vaccinated residents (vaccine strain mismatch). Rimantadine is an adamantane with high resistance; foscarnet and ganciclovir are anti-CMV.

Valacyclovir (oral prodrug of acyclovir) is first-line for genital herpes (HSV-2) — it reduces lesions, shedding and transmission. Lamivudine is anti-HIV, ribavirin anti-RSV/HCV, zanamivir anti-influenza.
Interferon alfa is an established treatment for chronic hepatitis B (pegylated IFN-alfa). Acyclovir is anti-herpes, zidovudine anti-HIV, and telaprevir is an HCV protease inhibitor (not for HBV).

Aerosolized ribavirin is a nucleoside analogue and the drug of choice for RSV infection in infants/young children. Entecavir and lamivudine are hepatitis drugs; palivizumab is a monoclonal antibody for RSV prophylaxis (not treatment).
The standard-of-care (of that era) for chronic HCV was pegylated interferon alfa plus ribavirin. Amantadine/acyclovir, foscarnet/vidarabine and lopinavir/ritonavir (anti-HIV) are not HCV treatments.

Oral valacyclovir (bid dosing) is the treatment of choice for herpes zoster (shingles) — it speeds healing and reduces post-herpetic neuralgia. Foscarnet is for acyclovir-resistant HSV/VZV; oseltamivir is anti-influenza.

Valganciclovir (oral, bioavailable prodrug of ganciclovir) is the drug of choice for CMV disease (retinitis/colitis) in HIV patients. Acyclovir has poor anti-CMV activity; foscarnet is second-line (i.v.); zanamivir is anti-influenza.

a.answer: For prevention of mother to child transmission
a.explanation: Tenofovir + lamivudine + dolutegravir (TLD) IS the first-line ART regimen for HIV-positive adults in Kenya, reduces opportunistic infections, and increases survival — but dolutegravir was historically avoided/not recommended for PMTCT in pregnancy (neural tube defect concern at conception), so TLD was not used for this indication at the time the question was set.

b.modelAnswer:
a) MANAGEMENT (4 marks):
1. Uncomplicated malaria: treat with an artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) — e.g., artemether-lumefantrine (or dihydroartemisinin-piperaquine) for 3 days.
2. Cryptococcal meningitis: induction therapy with IV amphotericin B + oral flucytosine for 2 weeks (fluconazole if flucytosine unavailable), followed by consolidation and maintenance with oral fluconazole.
3. HIV: continue/initiate combination ART (e.g., TLD) — starting ART about 2 weeks after antifungal therapy to reduce immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) risk.
b) MODE OF ACTION OF EACH DRUG (8 marks):
- Artemether (artemisinin derivative): activated by parasite iron/ferrous heme → free radicals damage parasite membranes and proteins — fast-acting blood schizonticide.
- Lumefantrine: blood schizonticide that complexes with heme, preventing its detoxification — acts as the longer-acting partner drug.
- Amphotericin B: polyene that binds ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane → forms pores → leakage of cellular contents → cell death (fungicidal).
- Flucytosine: taken up by fungal cytosine permease → converted to 5-fluorouracil → inhibits thymidylate synthase and incorporates into RNA/DNA → disrupts nucleic acid synthesis.
- Fluconazole: azole that inhibits fungal 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51) → blocks ergosterol synthesis → membrane dysfunction (fungistatic).
c) ONE SIDE EFFECT OF EACH (4 marks): Artemether-lumefantrine — QT prolongation/GI upset; Amphotericin B — nephrotoxicity (or infusion reactions, hypokalemia); Flucytosine — bone marrow suppression (or GI upset); Fluconazole — hepatotoxicity (or GI upset, rash).
d) WHY ATAZANAVIR IS COMBINED WITH RITONAVIR (2 marks): Ritonavir is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor used as a pharmacokinetic booster — it inhibits the metabolism of atazanavir, raising its plasma levels, allowing once-daily dosing, smaller pill burden and lower cost, without adding significant antiviral activity at the boosting dose.
e) FOUR CLINICAL APPLICATIONS OF ALBENDAZOLE (2 marks): Ascariasis; hookworm infection (Necator/Ancylostoma); enterobiasis (pinworm); trichuriasis (whipworm); also: hydatid disease (Echinococcus), neurocysticercosis, strongyloidiasis, cutaneous larva migrans. (Any four.)

c.modelAnswer:
GENERAL LIFE CYCLE OF VIRUSES AND HOW DRUGS TARGET EACH PHASE (10 marks):
1. ATTACHMENT to host cell receptors — HIV gp120 binds CD4 + co-receptor (CCR5/CXCR4). Drug: Maraviroc — CCR5 co-receptor antagonist blocks attachment of CCR5-tropic HIV.
2. FUSION/ENTRY — viral envelope fuses with the cell membrane. Drug: Enfuvirtide — gp41 fusion inhibitor peptide prevents membrane fusion of HIV.
3. UNCOATING — release of viral genome. Drug: Amantadine/Rimantadine — block the M2 ion channel of influenza A, preventing acid-dependent uncoating.
4. REVERSE TRANSCRIPTION (retroviruses) — RNA → DNA. Drugs: NRTIs (zidovudine, tenofovir, lamivudine) — chain terminators after intracellular phosphorylation, competitively inhibit RT; NNRTIs (nevirapine, efavirenz) — non-competitive binding to RT, no phosphorylation required.
5. INTEGRATION — viral DNA inserted into host genome. Drug: Raltegravir/Dolutegravir — integrase strand-transfer inhibitors.
6. TRANSCRIPTION/TRANSLATION of viral proteins — interferons (immunomodulatory, antiviral); not a major direct drug target in common use.
7. PROTEASE CLEAVAGE/ASSEMBLY — viral polyprotein cleaved into functional proteins. Drugs: Protease inhibitors (ritonavir, lopinavir, atazanavir) — inhibit HIV aspartyl protease, producing non-infectious immature virions.
8. RELEASE/BUDDING — new virions leave the cell. Drugs: Oseltamivir/Zanamivir — neuraminidase inhibitors block release of influenza virions from the infected cell surface.
CLINICAL APPLICATIONS (5 marks): Maraviroc — CCR5-tropic HIV-1 (treatment-experienced); Enfuvirtide — salvage therapy for multidrug-resistant HIV; Amantadine — influenza A (now rarely used due to resistance); Zidovudine/Tenofovir/Lamivudine — HIV infection (first-line NRTI backbone) and tenofovir also in HBV; Nevirapine — HIV (and historically PMTCT single-dose); Raltegravir/Dolutegravir — HIV first-line/switch therapy; Ritonavir/Lopinavir/Atazanavir — HIV treatment (ritonavir also as booster); Oseltamivir/Zanamivir — treatment and prophylaxis of influenza A/B.
TWO ADVERSE EFFECTS OF EACH (5 marks): Maraviroc — hepatotoxicity, upper respiratory infections/cough, cardiovascular events; Enfuvirtide — injection-site reactions, hypersensitivity (rare); Amantadine — CNS effects (insomnia, nervousness, hallucinations), anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention); Zidovudine — bone marrow suppression (anemia/neutropenia), GI intolerance, myopathy; Tenofovir — nephrotoxicity (Fanconi syndrome), decreased bone mineral density; Lamivudine — generally well tolerated: headache, nausea, rare pancreatitis; Nevirapine — severe skin rash (SJS), hepatotoxicity; Raltegravir — headache, insomnia, nausea, rare myopathy/rhabdomyolysis; Ritonavir/Lopinavir — GI intolerance (diarrhea, nausea), hyperlipidemia, lipodystrophy, insulin resistance; Atazanavir — hyperbilirubinemia/jaundice, nephrolithiasis, QT prolongation; Oseltamivir — nausea/vomiting, headache, rare neuropsychiatric events; Zanamivir — bronchospasm (avoid in asthma), cough, nasal discomfort.

HOW DRUGS TARGET ERGOSTEROL (6 marks):
1. BINDING TO ERGOSTEROL (polyenes) — Amphotericin B and Nystatin bind ergosterol in the fungal cell membrane, forming pores/channels → leakage of ions and cellular contents → cell death (fungicidal). Example: amphotericin B for systemic mycoses.
2. INHIBITION OF ERGOSTEROL SYNTHESIS (azoles) — Ketoconazole, Fluconazole, Itraconazole, Voriconazole inhibit 14-alpha-demethylase (CYP51), blocking conversion of lanosterol to ergosterol and causing accumulation of toxic 14-methyl sterols → defective membrane (fungistatic). Example: fluconazole for candidiasis/cryptococcosis.
3. INHIBITION OF SQUALENE EPOXIDASE (allylamines) — Terbinafine blocks squalene epoxidase, preventing squalene → lanosterol conversion; toxic squalene accumulates and ergosterol is depleted → fungicidal. Example: terbinafine for dermatophyte (nail/skin) infections.
CLINICAL APPLICATIONS (4 marks): Amphotericin B — severe systemic mycoses: cryptococcal meningitis (induction), invasive candidiasis, histoplasmosis, aspergillosis, mucormycosis; Nystatin — topical/oral candidiasis (thrush, vaginal, skin); Fluconazole — mucosal and systemic candidiasis, cryptococcal meningitis (consolidation/maintenance), dermatophytosis; Itraconazole — dermatophytosis, blastomycosis, histoplasmosis, onychomycosis; Voriconazole — invasive aspergillosis (DOC), candidemia, Scedosporium; Ketoconazole — topical dermatophytosis/candidiasis (oral use limited by toxicity); Terbinafine — onychomycosis, tinea infections (athlete's foot, ringworm).
TWO SIDE EFFECTS OF EACH (6 marks): Amphotericin B — nephrotoxicity, infusion-related reactions (fever, chills, hypotension), hypokalemia/hypomagnesemia; Nystatin — (topical, few systemic): local irritation, nausea (oral suspension), taste disturbance; Fluconazole — hepatotoxicity, GI upset, rash; Itraconazole — hepatotoxicity, heart failure/negative inotropy, GI upset, edema; Voriconazole — visual disturbances (photopsia), hepatotoxicity, photosensitivity, QT prolongation; Ketoconazole — hepatotoxicity, adrenal suppression/gynecomastia (CYP inhibition of steroids), GI upset; Terbinafine — GI upset, skin rash, taste disturbance, rare hepatotoxicity.
TWO DRUG-DRUG INTERACTIONS (4 marks):
1. Azoles inhibit CYP450: ketoconazole/fluconazole + warfarin → reduced warfarin metabolism → bleeding (raised INR); azoles + astemizole/terfenadine/cisapride → QT prolongation/torsades de pointes; azoles + statins → myopathy/rhabdomyolysis (e.g., itraconazole + simvastatin).
2. Amphotericin B: additive nephrotoxicity with aminoglycosides, cyclosporine, cisplatin, foscarnet; hypokalemia potentiated by corticosteroids/diuretics (risk of cardiac arrhythmia).
3. Terbinafine inhibits CYP2D6 → increased levels of tricyclic antidepressants, SSRIs, beta-blockers.
(Any two well-described interactions.)
